title: A Punjabi-speaking state, 1966
hook: after long campaigning, a smaller Punjab is formed around the Punjabi language
tomorrow: The daily prayer for open doors

segments.voice: Yesterday, starting again: chardi kala, again. Today the rebuilding turns to something you can't carry in a bundle: a language.

Some words don't survive translation. A grandmother's scolding in the language she grew up with. A family's private switch of tongue when the kids shouldn't follow. The name of a dish. The way people say goodbye at the door. A language carries all of that, which is why people will campaign for years to keep one. In the 1950s, India's map was being redrawn around languages, state by state. Punjabi speakers asked for a state of their own, and were told no.
screen: `WORDS THAT DON'T TRANSLATE.` → `THE MAP REDRAWN BY LANGUAGE.` → `PUNJABI SPEAKERS TOLD NO.`

segments.voice: After independence, Telugu speakers got a state of their own, and so did others. But when Sikh leaders asked for one built around Punjabi, the answer was no, for years. The campaign was called the Punjabi Suba movement, suba meaning a province. It was led by the Akali Dal, first under Master Tara Singh and later under Sant Fateh Singh. Its main tool was the morcha: a peaceful campaign in which volunteers marched, sang and courted arrest, wave after wave. Tens of thousands went to jail. Language had become tangled with religion and politics. Punjabi written in Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib, was close to Sikh hearts. In the censuses of those years, many Punjabi-speaking Hindus, urged on by some Hindu organizations, recorded Hindi as their language instead. So the question was never only about grammar. Then, in 1966, after the war with Pakistan the year before, the government agreed. On the first of November 1966, Punjab was divided again, this time peacefully. The Hindi-speaking south became a new state, Haryana. Hill districts went to Himachal Pradesh. What remained was a smaller Punjab, with Punjabi in Gurmukhi as its language and Chandigarh held back as a shared capital. Not everyone was satisfied: arguments over Chandigarh and the river waters went on for decades, and they matter for the harder chapters ahead. But the language itself was kept: offices, street signs and school books in Punjabi, written in the script of the Guru Granth Sahib.
screen: `STATES REDRAWN BY LANGUAGE.` · `THE PUNJABI SUBA MOVEMENT.` · `PEACEFUL MORCHAS, THOUSANDS JAILED.` · `NOVEMBER 1, 1966: A SMALLER PUNJAB.` · then, large: `THE LANGUAGE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Find one word from the language you grew up with, or the one your family spoke before you, maybe a word for grandmother, or bread, or home, and say it quietly, once. If you only have one language, find a word that belongs to your family alone, a nickname or a saying. Notice who it brings to mind, and let it keep you company for a few breaths.
Punjabi suba. The movement for a Punjabi-speaking province, which won, on November 1, 1966, a smaller Punjab with Punjabi in Gurmukhi as its language.
Your line: the language kept. Some things can't be carried in a bundle, only spoken. That's day three hundred three.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Punjabi Suba movement as a long, largely peaceful campaign; many gurdwaras still teach Gurmukhi so that Punjabi, the language of the Guru Granth Sahib's script, is kept.
